\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{كبد} (kabid)}{كبد (kabid)}]{\ar{كبد} (kabid) — the liver}

\label{lesson:AR-C504-kabid}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for organized, then the Arabic for careless.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{كبد}}
\textbf{\ar{كبد}} — \emph{kabid} — \textquotedblleft{}the liver\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{أكل} \ar{جدي} \ar{كبد} \ar{الخروف}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{akala jaddī kabid al-kharūf.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
My grandfather ate the sheep's liver.
\end{quote}

Plural: \ar{أكباد}, \emph{akbād}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{كبد}} (\emph{kabid}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{k-b-d}, \textquotedblleft{}the liver\textquotedblright{} (Lane). The word is old; its plural is akbād.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kabid}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kabid}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{akala jaddī kabid al-kharūf.} — My grandfather ate the sheep's liver.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for organized, then the Arabic for careless, then say \emph{kabid} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{كبد} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The liver\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{طحال} (ṭiḥāl)}{طحال (ṭiḥāl)}]{\ar{طحال} (ṭiḥāl) — the spleen}

\label{lesson:AR-C504-tihal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for careless, then the Arabic for the liver.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{طحال}}
\textbf{\ar{طحال}} — \emph{ṭiḥāl} — \textquotedblleft{}the spleen\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{الطحال} \ar{عضو} \ar{صغير} \ar{في} \ar{البطن}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{aṭ-ṭiḥāl ʿuḍw ṣaghīr fī al-baṭn.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The spleen is a small organ in the belly.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{طحال}} (\emph{ṭiḥāl}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{ṭ-ḥ-l}, \textquotedblleft{}to hurt the spleen\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Lane gives ṭaḥala as to strike or hurt the ṭiḥāl.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ṭiḥāl}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aṭ-ṭiḥāl ʿuḍw ṣaghīr fī al-baṭn.} — The spleen is a small organ in the belly.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for careless, then the Arabic for the liver, then say \emph{ṭiḥāl} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{معدة} (miʿda)}{معدة (miʿda)}]{\ar{معدة} (miʿda) — the stomach}

\label{lesson:AR-C504-mida}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for the liver, then the Arabic for the spleen.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{معدة}}
\textbf{\ar{معدة}} — \emph{miʿda} — \textquotedblleft{}the stomach\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{عندي} \ar{ألم} \ar{في} \ar{المعدة}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{ʿindī alam fī al-miʿda.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
I have a pain in my stomach.
\end{quote}

Baṭn, belly, is the outside; miʿda is the organ.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{معدة}} (\emph{miʿda}) is an old native Arabic word for the stomach, usually traced to the root \emph{m-ʿ-d}; the origin of the sense is not settled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{miʿda}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{miʿda}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ʿindī alam fī al-miʿda.} — I have a pain in my stomach.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for the liver, then the Arabic for the spleen, then say \emph{miʿda} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{معدة} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The stomach\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{أمعاء} (amʿāʾ)}{أمعاء (amʿāʾ)}]{\ar{أمعاء} (amʿāʾ) — the intestines, the bowels}

\label{lesson:AR-C504-ama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for the spleen, then the Arabic for the stomach.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{أمعاء}}
\textbf{\ar{أمعاء}} — \emph{amʿāʾ} — \textquotedblleft{}the intestines, the bowels\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{الأمعاء} \ar{طويلة} \ar{جدا}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{al-amʿāʾ ṭawīla jiddan.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The intestines are very long.
\end{quote}

It is a plural; the singular \ar{معى} is rare in daily speech.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{أمعاء}} (\emph{amʿāʾ}) is the plural of \emph{miʿan}, a gut, and is built on the native Arabic root \emph{m-ʿ-y} (Lane). The plural pattern \emph{afʿāl} (as in \emph{akhbār}) is common for short nouns.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{amʿāʾ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{amʿāʾ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{al-amʿāʾ ṭawīla jiddan.} — The intestines are very long.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for the spleen, then the Arabic for the stomach, then say \emph{amʿāʾ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{أمعاء} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The intestines, the bowels\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\ar{نبض} (nabḍ)}{نبض (nabḍ)}]{\ar{نبض} (nabḍ) — the pulse}

\label{lesson:AR-C504-nabd}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Arabic for the stomach, then the Arabic for the intestines.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{نبض}}
\textbf{\ar{نبض}} — \emph{nabḍ} — \textquotedblleft{}the pulse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
\ar{فحص} \ar{الطبيب} \ar{نبض} \ar{المريض}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{faḥaṣa aṭ-ṭabīb nabḍ al-marīḍ.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
The doctor checked the patient's pulse.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{نبض}} (\emph{nabḍ}) is built on the native Arabic root \emph{n-b-ḍ}, \textquotedblleft{}to beat, to throb\textquotedblright{} (Lane). Nabḍ is each beat of the blood.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for describing what you lived and felt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nabḍ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nabḍ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{faḥaṣa aṭ-ṭabīb nabḍ al-marīḍ.} — The doctor checked the patient's pulse.
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Arabic for the stomach, then the Arabic for the intestines, then say \emph{nabḍ} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ar{نبض} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The pulse\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
